acceptance.text: End to end on a fixture repo, with a stub model that makes a correct change: a PR is opened and the task is `in_review` with one attempt logged.
A stub model that fails three times → `needs_human` with `attempts_exhausted`, and no PR.
A quota/429 error stops `loop` and marks `quota_exhausted`, with no retry.
`loop` won't start a session during 08:00–12:00 Mon–Fri Swedish time. The window comes from config.
The code contains no `gh pr merge` call (a grep test).
Every attempt records `prompt_versions` (seat → prompt content hash, from F-09) and `skills` (the skills loaded). An attempt without them is a schema error.
The PR body has these sections: **Summary**, **Evidence**, **Merge Danger** (Door + Blast Radius), **Contract**, **Validator report**. The PR isn't opened if any is missing.

**Evidence** is built by the orchestrator from the L1 report, not from model text. For each contract test ref it shows red on base (with `red_reason`) and green on head. Nothing the implementer writes can alter this section.

**Door** is `one-way` when the task carries any of `migration`, `deploy`, `external_service`, `payments` or `privacy` (data that has leaked can't be recalled), and `two-way` otherwise. **Blast Radius** lists the risk flags and matched `paths.risk` globs, or `contained`. The implementer may add prose below them but can't change either value.

An attempt that starts in a fresh session (re-queued run, rejected-PR fix round) receives the task's progress log, entries 1..N. The log is orchestrator-owned, lives outside the clone and is append-only: rewriting an earlier entry raises.

L0 and L1 run every project command (setup, lint, typecheck, test, and each `test_ref`) inside the F-05 sandbox via `run_sandboxed` on the clean clone, never in the orchestrator's own environment: the agent's `conftest.py` and test code are untrusted. A fixture whose `conftest.py` tries to write outside the run dir and read `~/factory/holdouts` is denied both during the L0 test gate and the L1 red/green runs.

Every run dir `run` creates is removed with `cleanup_run` on every outcome (PR opened, `needs_human`, quota stop, exception), together with its settings, staged runner and scratch. `loop` reclaims, at start, run dirs no live run lease holds. A run killed mid-session is cleaned up by the next `loop` start.

The orchestrator never pushes to the default branch: the push refspec names only the task's own branch, and a push targeting `repo.default_branch`, or any ref the run didn't create, raises before any git process starts. Every orchestrator-side git call uses `GIT_HARDENING`. (The factory's own repo can't have branch protection on a free private plan, so this check is the only guard on its `main`.)

The PR body also carries a **How to revert** section, built by the orchestrator: for a `two-way` Door, revert the squash-merge commit; for a `one-way` Door, a statement that reverting the code doesn't undo the listed risk flags, naming each one. The PR isn't opened without it (same rule as AC-7).
For a fixture `tasks.json`, the summary lists every `needs_human` task with its escalation reason.
Metrics computed from `attempts` match hand-computed values for the fixture.

The summary reports outcome measures only (RESEARCH-SOFTWARE-FACTORY §9): interventions per task, review rounds per attempt, tokens per merged PR, time from approval to merge, and the share of merged factory PRs later reverted (a revert commit naming the PR's merge commit). It never reports lines of code or PR counts as a measure of success.

The output validates against the schema, or the import is refused.
Every imported task is `draft`.
Running it twice with no doc changes proposes no diff for existing tasks. Status and attempts are preserved.

The importer reads `.factory/out-of-scope/` (TASK-CONTRACT §5). A proposed task that resembles a record is listed in the import summary with the record's path. It's still proposed as `draft` and is never dropped or rejected on its own: you confirm the match.

Edits are additions, removals or changes to individual items, never whole-file rewrites (a diff-size check).

The weekly review groups failed and escalated attempts by `prompt_versions` and `skills`, and reports each version's failure share. Each proposed edit names the version it targets and the evidence (attempt run ids) behind it.

tasks.title: Vetted agent toolkit (skills, plugins, MCP servers)

acceptance.text: A toolkit index (`toolkit/index.yaml`, schema-validated on every load) lists each admitted item: kind (`skill`, `plugin` or `mcp_server`), name, upstream repo, pinned commit SHA (or package version plus integrity hash), SPDX licence, content hash, and the path of its vetting report. Vendored files live under `toolkit/` next to their upstream LICENSE. A vendored file whose content no longer matches its index hash is refused at load.

Licence gate: only allowlisted licences (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC) are admitted. A skill whose licence is missing or proprietary (for example "All rights reserved", as on Anthropic's document skills) is refused, with the reason named.

`factory toolkit vet <path>` scans every file of a candidate, prompts and scripts alike, and fails on each of these classes: outbound network calls or URLs outside the project's allowlists; shell execution, eval or exec; encoded blobs above a size threshold; reads of credential locations (`~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `.env`, the macOS keychain via `security`); environment-variable harvesting; hidden characters (zero-width, bidi overrides, Unicode tag characters); prompt-injection phrasing (instructions to ignore earlier instructions, to hide actions from the user, or to exfiltrate); self-modification or auto-update. A seeded fixture for each class is flagged, and a clean fixture passes.

Admission is human: an item enters the index only through a PR carrying its vetting report, approved by the owner. A clean scan never admits on its own, and any version bump repeats the full vet. Aggregators (awesome lists, mcpmarket, the GitHub MCP Registry) are discovery sources only: the index always pins the real upstream repo.

MCP servers are admitted only when read-only (no tool that writes, sends or deploys), with no credentials in their environment, every network domain they need inside the project's allowlists, and a pinned version with an integrity hash. They run inside the session's sandbox, and their tools are enabled one by one through `allowed_tools`. A descriptor that needs a credential or exposes a write tool is refused.

Each project chooses its toolkit in `project.yaml` (`toolkit: {skills, plugins, mcp_servers}`, optionally narrowed per seat, so the reviewer can get a read-only subset). Every name must be an index entry, and an unknown or unvetted name refuses the profile at load, as F-02 does for invalid state.

A session gets exactly its project's toolkit and nothing from the owner's personal Claude setup. The test plants a skill and an MCP server in a fake personal config and asserts neither is visible, while every listed item is. The toolkit is loaded from a read-only staged copy outside the clone (the F-06 runner-staging pattern).
Every attempt's `skills` records what actually loaded, as `<name>@<content-hash>` (replacing the hardcoded empty list), so F-19 can attribute failures to toolkit versions.

The first JobFinderOS toolkit goes through the whole process end to end: one vetted skill (strict-api, vendored from `alirezarezvani/claude-skills` @ `0496583`, MIT), admitted by owner-approved PR, with its report committed. A JobFinderOS session test shows the skill available. *(Re-scoped 2026-10-30, owner-directed — the F-27 AC-4 precedent. Original text promised a read-only documentation MCP server in the same toolkit; the Phase-1 evaluation found no upstream docs MCP server that passes the spawn/env allowlists — context7-mcp (published dist needs external node packages), pypi-docs-mcp (httpx/bs4 absent from the session interpreter, arbitrary-URL tool, GitHub API hosts), docs-mcp-server (native deps, arbitrary-URL fetching), python-docs-mcp (pins mcp<2.0 vs the interpreter's 2.3.0, docs.python.org unallowlisted), pg-aiguide (Bun/TS RAG service on a credentialed LLM API). The MCP half is deferred to F-39 rather than bending the rules.)*

Every L2 finding is stored per attempt with a stable key (file, rule or category, normalised summary). A finding whose key was raised in an earlier round and is unchanged in the diff since is not re-raised; the reviewer's verdict lists it as carried, not new.

Rounds after the first give the reviewer the delta since the last reviewed sha as primary scope, with the full diff for reference only. A new finding outside the delta must say why it was missed earlier, or it is dropped as out of scope.
The implementer's fix prompt carries each finding with an instruction to find and fix sibling sites of the same defect class, and the next round's reviewer checks for siblings explicitly.

No-progress stop: if a round's FAIL contains only findings whose keys were already raised and claimed fixed, the task escalates `review_not_converging` (added to the schema enum, red-first) instead of spending another round.

A fixture project (built by the test, no network) has a setup that installs a Python venv and a `node_modules` tree, declared as `setup_outputs`; a remote whose default branch is ahead of the local clone; and an ambient `PATH` that includes home-dir entries.
A rehearsal test runs setup, L0 and L1 over a one-criterion contract against that fixture, end to end through the real sandbox, and passes on `main`.

Reverting each PR #24 fix in turn (L1 `_clean` keeping setup outputs, `_path_outside_home`, `_build_on_remote_default`) makes the rehearsal fail. Proven by three tests that monkeypatch the old behaviour back in.
CI runs the rehearsal on every PR (it is not marked slow or optional).

`docs/incidents.md` records the three incidents, and for each: what broke, which layer should have caught it, and the test that now does. Every future factory incident adds an entry and a test in the same PR (checked by a test that every entry names an existing test).

L0 runs built-in sentinels on every diff and fails with the sentinel's name: a credential-shaped string added (key, token, private-key patterns); a new skip, xfail or `only` marker on an existing test; an assertion removed from an existing test without a replacement; a `# noqa`, `type: ignore` or lint-disable added on a line the diff also changed in a risk path.

`project.yaml` may add project sentinels under `sentinels.<risk flag>` (a list of command plus description), validated by the schema; `paths.risk` keeps its current shape. They run only when the diff touches that risk flag's globs, and a failure escalates `sentinel_failed` (schema enum, red-first).
Each built-in sentinel has a seeded fixture diff that it flags and a clean diff that it passes.
Sentinel results appear in the PR body and in the attempt record, pass or fail, so the human merge sees what was checked.

`factory run` and `factory loop` refuse to start on a repo whose default-branch protection does not require status checks with `strict` (up to date) enabled, naming the missing setting (checked via `gh api`, faked in tests). The one exception is a repo whose plan can't offer protection (GitHub answers the protection call with its plan-limit 403, e.g. a private repo on a free plan) and whose `project.yaml` declares `branch_protection: unavailable` (schema-validated enum, red-first). Then the factory enforces the equivalent itself: before it reports a factory PR ready or merges it, it fetches the remote default-branch head and checks that the PR branch contains it; if not, it re-validates per AC-3. The declaration never excuses a repo that could have protection but doesn't (protection call returns not-protected, or the declaration is missing): that still refuses, naming the setting.
The loop keeps at most one open factory PR per repo by default (`concurrency: 1` in `project.yaml`, schema-validated). A ready task waits while one is open.

When the default branch has moved past an open factory PR's base, `factory run` re-runs L0 and L1 on the PR merged onto the new base before reporting it ready; a failure moves the task to `needs_human` with escalation `stale_base` (schema enum, red-first).

Implementer and reviewer sessions have one extra tool, `vent(category, text)`, an in-process SDK tool listed in `allowed_tools`. Categories: missing_tool, unclear_contract, flaky_check, environment, other.
Each call appends one record (run id, task id, seat, turn, category, text) to the run's progress log outside the clone. The tool can write nothing else, and text is length-capped.
Venting never changes a run's outcome or budget (a test vents mid-run and asserts the attempt record is otherwise identical).
The week's vents are readable grouped by category through the read-only `weeks_vents` seam, whose docstring names its consumers: `factory status` (F-11) lists them, F-19's review reads them.

acceptance.text: `factory tick <id> <step> [<step> ...] --evidence <text>` shows each named owner step (1-based) and asks for confirmation per step. A confirmed step gets `done: true`, `done_at`, `done_by` and `evidence` (additive schema fields; `done: true` without the other three is refused at load). `--evidence` is required and non-blank; there is no `--yes`.

An unknown task, a step number out of range, an already-ticked step, a blank evidence string, or a declined confirmation each leaves `tasks.json` byte-identical and exits non-zero with a message naming the problem. One tick call is one atomic save: a refusal on any named step writes none of them.
Ticking the last open step of an `awaiting_owner` task moves it to `done` in the same save. Ticking a step of a task in any other status records the tick and never changes the status.

An `owner_only` task whose last step is ticked moves `draft → not_buildable → done` through two new table edges. Both are guarded: only a non-executable kind may enter `not_buildable` from `draft`, and only an `owner_only` task with at least one step and every step ticked may go `not_buildable → done`. A `build` or `docs` task taking either edge raises (one test per edge).
Reconcile leaves `owner_only` tasks untouched: the real-files reconcile tests assert F-00 is unchanged by the run, not that it is `draft`, so they keep passing after F-00 is ticked to `done`.

tasks.title: Run trace: live event log per run

acceptance.text: The orchestrator appends one event per line to `<factory_root>/trace/<project>/<run-id>.jsonl`, outside every clone and outside the sandbox's write allowlist (a test asserts the path is not writable from a session). Event types: `phase_start`/`phase_end` for setup, implementer, L0, L1, L2 and publish; `tool_call` (seat, tool name, args, result snippet, ok, started/ended); `gate_check` (layer, item, ok, note); `session_end` (seat, tokens by component, cost, turns, model). Every event carries run id, task id, attempt number and a sequence number.
Events are written as they happen. A test with a fake SDK stream asserts a `tool_call` line is on disk before the stream yields its `ResultMessage`.

Gate events carry evidence on pass and on fail: each L0 check, each L1 red/green proof and each L2 finding is one `gate_check` with a note saying what was looked at (one test per layer, both outcomes).

Secrets never reach the trace. Args and result snippets are length-capped, and the seat token value plus credential-shaped strings (the F-25 patterns) are replaced with `[redacted]` before the line is written. A test runs a fake tool call whose output contains the seat token and asserts the token appears nowhere in the file.

Tracing never changes a run. A trace write that fails (disk full, permission) is reported once and the run continues; a test makes every write raise and asserts the attempt record is identical to an untraced run.
`factory trace <run-id> [--follow]` prints the trace in order, one line per event; `--follow` keeps printing new events until the attempt ends (published, failed or aborted). It reads only.
Per-phase token totals in the trace sum to the attempt's token totals in `tasks.json` for a fixture run (no second source of truth for spend).

`factory dashboard [--port N]` serves on `127.0.0.1` only (a test asserts the bound address), using the standard library's `http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer` and static files shipped in the package. No new dependency. A test holds one event stream open and asserts a second request is still answered.

The server answers `GET` only; every other method gets 405. Every route checks the `Host` header: anything other than `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` gets 403 (DNS rebinding), with one test per route. A test runs every route against a fixture factory root and asserts no file under it changed (mtime and hash).

Queue view: every task grouped by status, with escalation reasons for `needs_human` and the open steps for `awaiting_owner`, read from `tasks.json` after schema validation (invalid state shows an error page, never partial data).

Run view: phases as swim lanes on a time axis, tool calls inside each lane, gate checks with their evidence, tokens and cost per phase, from the F-30 trace. A running task updates live over `GET /runs/<run-id>/events`, a server-sent event stream fed by the same follower as `factory trace --follow` (same stop conditions: `run_end`, a run that is no longer live, a pruned trace); the page falls back to polling if the stream drops. A test appends events to a fixture trace and asserts the stream delivers them in order and closes on `run_end`.
Metrics come from the F-11 functions, not a second implementation: for the F-11 fixture, the dashboard's numbers equal `factory status` output (one test).
Paths in the URL are run ids and task ids matched against the schema's id patterns; anything else is a 404. A test asserts `..` and absolute paths cannot read outside the factory root.
`GET /healthz` returns 200 with body `ok` without reading the queue or any trace, so a smoke test (and F-35's confirm flow) can tell a dead server from a broken queue.

acceptance.text: After an L0 or L1 failure, the orchestrator resumes the implementer's session by id and sends the numbered findings (same format as the progress log), up to `budget.max_corrections` per attempt (schema field, default 2, red-first). The resumed session runs in the same clone under the same sandbox settings as the first turn; a test asserts the settings file and run dir are unchanged between turns. Corrections count against the attempt's `max_turns` and wall clock.

It falls back to today's fresh session plus progress log when the session cannot be resumed, its budget is spent, or the failure is in L2. A test covers each fallback reason and asserts the progress log gets the same entries either way.
L2 never runs in a resumed implementer session: a test asserts the reviewer seat always starts fresh with its own options.
The attempt record and the F-30 trace carry each correction (number, findings sent, tokens spent), so F-11 can compare tokens per merged PR before and after this WO.

Resumed context and correction evidence never come from a file the session can write. The SDK session transcript lives under the session's writable HOME scratch (`<run_dir>/.home/.claude/projects/…/<session-id>.jsonl`; checked 2026-10-21 by running the CLI with a throwaway `HOME`), so the orchestrator copies it outside the sandbox write allowlist when each turn ends, and resumes only from that copy (or rebuilds from the F-30 trace). A test edits the in-sandbox transcript between turns and asserts the resumed session doesn't see the edit. F-19 AC-4 reads transcripts from the same copy.
A benign corpus of at least 20 real merged diffs (this repo's merged PRs, stored as patch files named by PR number) on which every built-in sentinel passes: zero findings across the corpus.

An attack corpus with at least one diff per built-in sentinel that the sentinel flags, kept separate from the F-25 AC-3 seed fixtures (separate files, written fresh), so tuning a pattern to its own seed can't hide a regression.

CI runs every built-in sentinel over both corpora on every PR. A sentinel in `BUILTIN_SENTINELS` with no attack diff, a hit on a benign diff, or a missed attack fails the run, naming the sentinel and the corpus file.

`factory sentinels replay [--corpus benign|attack] [<patch> ...]` runs the built-in sentinels over corpus diffs and prints one line per sentinel per diff. It reads only: a test asserts no file under the factory root changes.
The corpus directory is added to `paths.protected` in this repo's `.factory/project.yaml` (in the same PR), so a session can't edit the evidence that judges its sentinels.

`factory dashboard --operator` adds a chat panel and one POST route, `POST /operator/chat`. Every operator POST route is listed in one declared set in the dashboard module, which later work orders extend in their own code (F-35's `/operator/confirm`, F-37's inbox upload), never by editing `tests/test_f34.py`; every route in the set enforces AC-2. Without `--operator`, F-31 AC-2 holds unchanged (GET only, everything else 405); a test runs F-31's route sweep both ways and asserts, with `--operator`, that the routes accepting POST are exactly the declared set.

Every POST requires a per-launch random token embedded in the served page, a `Host` of exactly `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` (F-31 AC-2's set) and a matching `Origin`. A cross-site form post, a DNS-rebinding `Host` or a missing or wrong token gets 403 and starts no session (one test per case); a test drives one chat turn from a page served as `localhost`, end to end. The confirm half of that e2e lands with F-35's confirm route (F-35 AC-3), which enforces the same checks.

A new `operator` seat: read-only sandbox (`build_settings(read_only=True)`) with its network narrowed to the model provider's host — the profile's `docs_allowlist` and `network_allowlist`, which `build_settings` adds for the build seats today, are left out (a new `build_settings` option; a test asserts the seat's `allowedDomains` is exactly the model host). No GitHub token. Its tools are denied explicitly in `disallowed_tools`, because `allowed_tools` grants without restricting: Write, Edit, NotebookEdit, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch and Task (sub-agents) — WebSearch runs on the provider's side, outside srt's network confinement, so the sandbox alone cannot stop it. A test asserts the seat denies each of those tools. Reads are limited to the queue, traces, progress logs, reports and the repo. Its prompt `prompts/operator.md` is pinned like the other seats (F-09 AC-2).

`POST /operator/chat` starts the turn and returns its run id; the panel renders the turn from F-31's `GET /runs/<run-id>/events` stream, so chat has no second streaming path. Tool calls reach the trace through the same `_tap_tool_calls` path as F-30, with the same redaction (seat token plus F-25 shapes); every chat turn is a trace run under its own run id.

Transcripts are saved to `<factory_root>/operator/<session-id>.jsonl` (0600 file in a 0700 directory) and pruned by the F-30 retention window. A turn has a `max_turns` cap and a wall-clock limit from config; hitting either ends the turn with a visible message, never a hang.
The chat changes nothing: a test runs a scripted operator session against a fixture factory root and asserts every file outside `operator/` and `trace/` is byte-identical afterwards.

The operator seat gets one more in-process tool, `propose_action(kind, task_id, step?)`. Kinds are limited to `approve`, `tick` and `recover`. `run`, `loop`, merging and anything else is refused with a reason.

The proposal card is built by the server from `tasks.json`, never from the agent's text. `approve` shows `render_contract(task)`, the same text `factory approve` prints, with its `acceptance_hash`; `tick` shows the step text and an empty evidence box only you fill in. A test proves the agent's own description of a proposal never reaches the card.

Confirming is `POST /operator/confirm` with a one-time nonce bound to the proposal's kind, task id, step and `acceptance_hash`. A reused nonce, or one whose task changed since the card was shown, gets 409 and writes nothing. The confirm POST enforces F-34 AC-2's token, `Host` and `Origin` checks (403, one test per case), and the end-to-end test completes here: one confirm from a page served as `localhost`.

A confirmed action runs `approve_task`, `tick_steps` or `recover_task` with your click as the `confirm` callback, never `assume_yes`. Every existing refusal still applies (no acceptance items, already ticked, blank evidence, and so on) and shows on the card. Risk-flagged tasks need a second explicit checkbox, the click-level equivalent of F-04 AC-3's "always interactive".
No agent path can confirm: the operator seat has no route, tool or token that reaches `/operator/confirm`. A test drives a session that tries every tool and asserts the queue is unchanged.
Every proposal and every confirm or decline goes into the operator transcript and the F-30 trace, with who clicked and when.

The F-34 panel offers a `planner` seat (`POST /operator/chat` with `seat: planner`) with the operator's read-only sandbox and tool denials (F-34 AC-3). In-process tools run inside the sandboxed runner, so the planner's sandbox allows exactly the model host plus the project's `docs_allowlist` hosts (never `network_allowlist`), and with Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch and Task denied, `fetch_doc` is the planner's only path to those hosts. Documentation lookups go through that in-process `fetch_doc(url)` tool, which accepts only `https` URLs whose host is an exact member of the project's `docs_allowlist`, on the default port only (no explicit port other than 443), with a path of at most 256 bytes drawn from `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ /`; a URL carrying a query string or fragment is refused, not stripped, a redirect response is refused rather than followed, a session's fetch count is capped from config, every fetched URL is recorded in the trace, and the fetched body honors the same size cap and text types as an inbox upload with a timeout from config (one test per refusal: non-https scheme, query string, fragment, non-allowlisted host, explicit non-443 port, over-long path, disallowed path character, fetch cap reached, redirect; plus a test that the planner's sandbox `allowedDomains` is exactly the model host plus `docs_allowlist`). The path rules bound, not close, an outbound channel to allowlisted hosts, so `docs_allowlist` lists only documentation hosts whose access logs no third party reads — never a user-content or shared-hosting domain. Files you attach (a client brief, say) upload through a token-gated POST (F-34 AC-2) into `<factory_root>/plans/<project>/inbox/` (0600 files in 0700 directories), with a size cap from config and text types only — anything else is refused at upload. Inbox files and saved plans are pruned by the same retention window as operator transcripts (F-34 AC-5), and `factory plans purge <project>` deletes them on demand.

The planner's only write is an in-process `save_plan(name, markdown)` tool into `<factory_root>/plans/<project>/`, with `name` matched against `[a-z0-9-]+\.md` minus the reserved `decisions` and `index` names: `decisions.md` is yours alone, and `index.md` is regenerated by the factory after each save, so neither is planner-writable. `index.md` lists only each plan's file name, size and save time, never text from inside a plan, so planner-authored content cannot ride the index into every resumed prompt (AC-4); a test saves a plan whose first line is an instruction and asserts `index.md` does not contain it. A test asserts `save_plan` cannot write outside that directory (`..`, absolute paths, symlinks) or under either reserved name, and that after a scripted planning session the repo, `tasks.json`, every trace other than the session's own and every plans file other than the session's own saves and the regenerated `index.md` are byte-identical, and `index.md` equals the generator's output for the directory.

`propose_work_orders(tasks)` validates the proposed tasks against `schema/tasks.schema.json` and shows them in the panel as the same diff `factory import` (F-12) shows; your confirm writes them through F-12's write path as `draft` only. A proposal carrying any other status, approval fields or attempts is refused, and so is one naming a task id already in `tasks.json` (F-12 merges spec fields into existing ids; a planner proposal only adds). Confirming is F-35's `POST /operator/confirm` with one added kind, `work_orders` (F-35 AC-1's `propose_action` kinds are unchanged): its one-time nonce is bound to the hash of the proposed tasks and the hash of `tasks.json` when the card was shown, and a reused nonce, or a queue that changed since, gets 409 and writes nothing (one test per case), with F-35 AC-3's token, `Host` and `Origin` checks. Nothing reaches `tasks.json` without the click (test).

Planning resumes across days: a planner session for a project starts with that project's plan index and `decisions.md` from `<factory_root>/plans/<project>/`, and no other memory source. A test asserts a resumed session's prompt carries both. `decisions.md` changes only by your hand: no tool or route writes it — the planner drafts proposed decision entries as an ordinary plan and you add them to the file yourself — and a test asserts a scripted session leaves the file byte-identical.

The planner's model comes from config (`seats.planner.model`, defaulting to the factory default), so it can run on a stronger model than the builders. The trace records the model of every planner turn (test).

No path from the planner to approval: the planner seat has no tool, route or token that reaches F-35's confirm or `factory approve`, and a test drives a session that tries every tool and asserts no task changes status.

The orchestrator runs N reviewer sessions (config, default 2) over the same diff in parallel, each a fresh context, then a verifier pass over the union of findings: each finding is kept with the voter's reasoning or dropped; survivors are ranked and tagged important / nit / pre-existing.

Style-only and diagnostic findings are dropped before the verdict, and at most three nits (severity `minor` or `note`) reach the PR body — REVIEW.md's nit budget, mechanically enforced; `blocking` and `major` findings are never capped.
Dropped findings and the drop reason land in the attempt record, so F-19 can measure the reviewer noise the verifier removed.

The fan-out and the vote are tested with scripted reviewer and verifier sessions, no real model: findings two reviewers both report merge into one entry of the union, and a finding the verifier drops never reaches the verdict or the PR body (one test per case). Measuring catch quality on seeded-bug and known-clean diffs is F-16's job (F-16 AC-3), run against this reviewer after it lands; that eval needs real model sessions, so it never runs in routine CI.
`prompt_versions` records every reviewer and verifier prompt hash; the fan-out is inside the attempt's turn and wall-clock budget.

One admission path is chosen at spec approval and implemented: either (a) vendored-bundle provenance — a reproducible bundle built from a pinned upstream, its build command and pinned build tool recorded in the index entry, every bundled dependency's licence allowlisted and recorded — or (b) a minimal factory-owned stdio server using only `mcp` and the standard library, every outbound request's host inside the running profile's `docs_allowlist` (scripted test: a host outside the allowlist is never fetched). The chosen server's spawn tokens and env keys pass the F-22 allowlists mechanically, proven red-first on the refusal cases.

The vetter's network class no longer counts a URL inside a LICENSE/NOTICE file as a finding when it is the canonical licence URL of the declared SPDX licence — red-first: a candidate whose only finding is its own licence text's URL passes. (This is what blocked `frontend-design` from anthropics/skills: the Apache-2.0 text quotes `www.apache.org/licenses/`.)

The first docs MCP server is admitted through the F-22 process — vet report committed, owner-approved PR — and a JobFinderOS session test shows its read-only tools granted one by one through `allowed_tools` and enforced by the MCP guard hook (scripted, no model).

`project.yaml` gains an optional `toolchain` list (schema-validated, red-first): each entry is a binary name resolved on PATH, or an absolute or `~/` path to a binary or SDK `bin` directory. Absent, the sandbox's defaults are exactly today's `TOOLCHAIN_BINS`, proven by an unchanged-settings test.

Profile load refuses an entry that is `$HOME` itself, an ancestor of it, or inside a credential location (`~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config/gh`, `~/.gnupg`), naming the entry. A relative path or an entry that resolves to nothing is refused the same way.

A profile-listed tool under the denied home executes in the gate runner AND every session seat, proven on real srt with a fixture tool under a denied HOME, while a sibling file beside the tool's install stays unreadable: only what `_toolchain_allowread` re-allows becomes readable, never the parent. Nothing is added to `allowWrite`.

The gate runner's run-local venv stays Python-only in effect: a profile with no Python commands still gates end to end through the real runner (fixture project whose setup, lint and test use only the listed tool).

tasks.title: Final full review after fix rounds

acceptance.text: When an attempt's fix rounds have ended in an L2 pass and at least one earlier L2 round ran in that attempt, the orchestrator runs one final full review before publish: the configured N reviewers in fresh contexts over the complete `base...head` diff, with no delta section and no carried-findings suppression, then the verifier vote. A task that passes L2 on its first round skips it, because that review was already full.

The F-23 out-of-delta drop does not apply to the final review: a finding in a file the fix rounds never touched stands without a `missed_earlier` field. Only surviving `blocking` or `major` findings fail it. `minor` and `note` findings never fail it and reach the PR body within the nit budget.

A failed final review sends its findings to one more implementer round, followed by L0, L1 and a repeat of the final review. The repeat count is bounded by a config value (default 1). When it is exhausted the task escalates `review_not_converging`: nothing is published with an unresolved blocking or major finding.

The final review sits inside the attempt's turn and wall-clock budgets, sharing F-38's per-session turn rule. When the remaining budget can't fit it, the task escalates `budget_exhausted`: a run never skips the final review to publish in time.

The attempt record and the F-30 trace show that the final review ran, its findings and its verdict. An end-to-end scripted test proves the gap this closes: a fix round breaks untested code in a file outside its delta, the delta review misses it, the final review catches it, and no PR opens until it is fixed.

A surviving `major` finding fails an L2 round exactly as a `blocking` one does, on every round, in `apply_vote` and in `apply_convergence`: a PR never opens with a surviving major finding. F-31's run (2026-10-30) published with a confirmed major defect because only `blocking` failed a round. A declared pass does not override it. The F-23 convergence stops still apply, so a repeated major finding escalates `review_not_converging` and never loops. `REVIEW.md` and `prompts/reviewer.md` state the rule, and the prompt pin is updated.

tasks.title: Session hardening: attribution and sandbox-bypass attempts

acceptance.text: A commit on a task's branch whose message carries an AI attribution trailer or footer fails L0 with a named finding before anything is pushed: `Co-Authored-By` naming an AI author or an AI vendor address, and `Generated with` footers. The patterns live in one list, matched on the commit messages between the merge-base and head, on every round. A human `Co-Authored-By` passes. The implementer gets the finding in its fix round and rewrites its own branch history.

The publish step refuses a PR title or body carrying the same patterns, naming the match, so nothing reaches GitHub through either path. A squash commit therefore can't inherit a trailer from the branch.

Sessions start with the CLI's own attribution default switched off, proven by a test on the built options and settings for every seat. `prompts/implementer.md` states the rule, and the prompt pin is updated.

Every seat's PreToolUse hook denies a Bash call whose input sets `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` to true, for all seats, under `bypassPermissions`, with a reason telling the session the sandbox is not negotiable. A real-session proof shows the denial firing, and a test covers each seat.

Each denial lands in the F-30 trace and counts on the attempt record, and `factory status` shows the week's total, so repeated bypass attempts are visible to the owner rather than lost in a tool result.
The existing commits on `main` are not rewritten. The F-42 ledger entry records that decision and lists the five affected commits, so the history stays honest.

(C-1) The implementer notes, every L2 finding text and the L2 verdict JSON pass the seam before `build_pr_body`. A test plants the literal seat token and a bare `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=<value>` echo in each input and asserts neither reaches the rendered body.
(C-1) `check_pr_text` refuses a PR title or body that carries the literal seat token, naming the refusal without echoing the token — a second, independent fence before the push.
(M-8) Vent text and `sessions/unparsable-record-*.stdout.txt` dumps pass the same seam; a test plants the token in each and asserts it is absent on disk.
(m-16) Vent text, `factory status` output and trace lines printed to a terminal have ANSI/OSC/C0 control sequences stripped; a test covers screen-clear, OSC-8 link and cursor-move sequences.

(I-10) `redact_credentials` and the credential sentinel catch JWTs, `Bearer <token>` literals and unquoted YAML `password:` values: one F-33 attack diff per shape, and the F-33 benign corpus stays clean.
A test enumerates every orchestrator path that writes session-derived text off the machine or to the owner's terminal and asserts each calls the seam, so a new channel cannot skip it.

(M-1) Severity is canonicalized once at parse (`strip().lower()`, beside the axis canonicalization). A test merges `"Blocking"` with `"minor"` in both orders and asserts the merged finding is blocking and the verdict fail; `eval._count_blocking` is case-insensitive.

(m-10) `_extract_json` refuses output carrying more than one valid verdict object with differing verdicts, as an invalid verdict that takes the retry path. Tests cover FAIL-then-example-PASS and the reverse.
(m-8) `parse_test_count` reads the count from the runner's final summary line, not the maximum anywhere in the output; a test whose test prints `999999 passed` does not clear the floor.
(I-11) Removing a `pytest.raises` block counts as an assertion removal, with an F-33 attack diff and a clean benign corpus.
(M-5) The stale-PR sweep runs under `queue.idle_lease()`. A test races a sweep against `reclaim_runs` and asserts no live run dir is deleted.
(M-6) A failing progress-log append in `_sweep_escalation` no longer leaves the task in `in_review`: a test injects the failure and asserts the task reaches `needs_human` and the next run proceeds.

(M-7) Publish-side `git push`, `ls-remote` and `gh pr create` run with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and a timeout through the same wrapper as `_fetch_sha`; a test with a hanging fake remote asserts a timed-out `PublishError`.
(m-13) A `finish()` failure between `append_attempt` and the transition records exactly one attempt; a test injects the failure.
(m-14) `gh pr view` exiting 0 with non-object JSON (`null`) maps to the documented unresolvable PR state, not an `AttributeError`.
(I-3) Atomic queue writes fsync the parent directory after the rename; a test asserts the directory fsync call.
(I-4) The run-lease error names the holder only when that holder is alive and says the lock is stale otherwise; a test covers both.
(M-2) The attribution scan reads each commit's message separately (per sha), not by splitting one log on `\x1e`; a commit whose body embeds `\x1e` before a trailer is flagged.

(m-17) Attribution matching runs on NFKC-normalized text with zero-width characters removed and any number of connecting tokens; tests cover U+2010, a fullwidth colon and a zero-width space inside "claude".
(m-9) `lint_suppression_added` checks both the old and new path of a rename; a test renames `payments/x.py` to `utils/x.py` with an added `# noqa` and asserts the finding.

(M-4) Test-runner configuration (`**/conftest.py`, `pytest.ini`, `pyproject.toml`'s pytest table, `setup.cfg`'s pytest section) is protected by a schema-level default that a profile can only widen; every profile in the repo still validates.
(M-4) L1 treats a contract test that was not collected as a failure at both the red and the green end; a test using a conftest that sets `collect_ignore` asserts L1 fails.

tasks.title: Sandbox read boundary and toolkit staging

acceptance.text: (M-9) `denyRead` covers the factory root itself with explicit carve-outs for the run's own dir and srt; a test with `--factory-root` outside `$HOME` asserts a session cannot read `trace/`, `progress/` or `sessions/`.
(I-9) A drain that force-closes a `setsid` escapee writes an event to the trace and counts in `factory status`.
(I-2) The index-load MCP domain check validates against the vetted allowlist, not against itself; a test uses an index entry with an unvetted domain.
(I-19) MCP descriptor staging copies its files explicitly; a test asserts the staged set without relying on a copytree side effect.
(M-3) The eval's L2 path runs `apply_convergence` exactly as production does, through one shared function; a test asserts the eval and the orchestrator call the same symbol.
(m-12) The eval checks quota before parsing seats, as production does; a test asserts zero re-runs for a quota-hit seat.
(m-11) The clean-diff report line shows L0 and L1 as well as L2, so a clean diff that failed L0 renders as an L0 false positive.
(I-12) `factory eval --repeats N` runs each seed N times and reports mean and spread per metric (default N=3; the owner confirms the default and cadence at approval).
(manual) The F-16 seeded eval is re-run on the fixed pipeline and the new baseline is recorded as tick evidence; the old numbers were measured without convergence.

check.expect: owner tick evidence: the re-run baseline report

acceptance.text: (M-10) A CI test resolves every acceptance ref on every non-draft task to a real test function, using F-01's AST resolution; a typo'd ref on a `ready` task fails.
(m-3) Schema validation enforces `format: date-time`; a malformed timestamp is rejected.
(m-4) A planning-doc listing over 200 files ends with `+N more` and the proposal names the truncated docs.
(m-6) The fresh-queue import write holds the queue lock across the check and the write.
(m-7) A proposal that raises `RecursionError` takes the keep-refused-output path; the session output is saved.
(I-18) A proposal without a `project` key is refused.
(m-1) The dashboard `/metrics` page expands `~` in the profile's repo path; a test uses a `~`-relative profile.
(m-2) `factory status` survives a non-UTF-8 commit subject.
(m-5) An explicit `--config <path>` that does not exist is an error; only the default config path may be absent.

tasks.title: Importer robustness: per-task tool, repair turn, prose eval

acceptance.text: A `propose_task(task)` tool on the importer seat (the vent pattern, `factory/vent.py`) validates one task per call against the staged proposal schema and the import rules, and returns `accepted <id>` or every violation. Re-proposing an id replaces it; the accepted set is the proposal; zero calls falls back to the text answer. Tests cover accept, every-violation, replace, forbidden fields and the fallback.

A refused proposal from a real session gets ONE repair session (the saved output, the full violation list and the contract; no doc re-reading; a turn budget well under the import's) instead of a full re-run. Quota stops it, it is a trace event, and a failed repair names both saved files. Scripted-session tests cover success, failure, quota and a stub session (no repair).

A prose-docs fixture repo (three prose work orders with no contract-shaped content, one owner-only, one too big for size M) drives an offline test: a scripted session returning the 2026-11-05 broken shapes (risk as a string, boolean gates, `AC1` ids, check type `grep`, size `L`, `P0`) is refused with every violation and fixed by the repair path.

`factory eval --importer` runs one real import against the fixture on demand (never in routine CI) and reports schema validity, task count and whether the oversized work order was split; the owner runs it once and records the report.
