tasks.title: Linux sandbox host on Ubuntu 26.04 and red-CI guard

acceptance.text: The 26.04 failure is reproduced and its cause named (AppArmor userns profile, kernel capability rule, or bubblewrap/srt version), with a minimal repro recorded in the WO's ledger entry.

The sandbox runs on ubuntu-26.04 without weakening it: an srt upgrade or a documented host setting (sysctl or an AppArmor profile for bubblewrap). The `tests/test_f05.py` attack tests pass unchanged on 26.04.

CI runs the sandbox suite on both `ubuntu-24.04` and `ubuntu-26.04`, as separately named jobs, so a runner image change fails one named job instead of every test; the 24.04-only pin from PR #97 is removed or kept with a stated reason in the workflow.

`factory run` preflights the host: when the sandbox cannot create its nested user namespace, the run refuses before picking a task, with one error naming the missing setting, not a cascade of session failures. A test with a fake srt that exits with the setgroups error asserts the refusal.

With `repo.branch_protection: unavailable`, the factory self-enforces green CI as it already self-enforces up-to-date: `factory run` refuses to start while the default branch's latest CI run for HEAD failed, and the stale-PR sweep never reports a PR ready whose checks fail. Tests cover a red default branch and a red PR, through the existing `pr_state`/protection seams.
README's and CLAUDE.md's host table lists exactly the hosts CI verifies; a test asserts every Ubuntu version in that table appears as a CI job.

Nesting is detected on Linux too: a suite run inside the srt sandbox on Linux skips its sandbox-spawning tests through the INC-007 guard instead of failing. The macOS-only skip PR #97 put on `test_nested_suite_skips_instead_of_failing` is removed, and that test passes on ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-26.04 and macOS.

tasks.title: Per-project model provider and provider record

acceptance.text: `project.yaml` gains `data_owner` (`self` | `client`) and a `provider` block: `kind` (`zai` | `anthropic` | `bedrock` | `vertex` | `anthropic_compatible`), a `model` per seat (implementer, reviewer, verifier, importer), `region` (required for bedrock/vertex), `base_url` (required for and only allowed with `anthropic_compatible`, https only). Schema-validated on load (F-02). A `client` project with no explicit `provider`, or with `kind: zai`, refuses to load, with the reason named; a `self` project with no block keeps today's Z.ai default. Tests cover every kind, each missing-field case and both refusals.

Credentials are per provider: one keychain item per kind (`factory-<kind>`), with the env lookup rule `seat_token` applies today generalised. A token is used only with its own provider's endpoint, never sent to another, and a token exported for one provider is refused when the project names another. `session_env` stays literal: for each kind it returns exactly the variable names that provider needs per the Agent SDK docs (for Bedrock a scoped bearer token or short-lived credentials plus the region; never the owner's ambient `~/.aws` profile or files). Tests assert the exact env key set per kind, the cross-provider refusal, and that no ambient `ANTHROPIC_*`/`AWS_*` value leaks in.

Session egress follows the provider: the sandbox network allowlist for a session contains the configured provider's inference host(s) (derived from kind, region or base_url) and no other model endpoint. A `client` project's session cannot reach the Z.ai host. Tests read the generated srt settings for each kind.

Every session record and attempt carries a provider record: kind, model id, region or endpoint host (never the token), and token usage (input, cache-read, cache-write, output). The task schema gains the fields, and `factory status` shows per-project, per-provider token totals and an estimated cost from an owner-maintained price table in the factory config (a missing price shows `n/a`, never 0). Tests cover the record, the schema, the total, and the missing-price case.

Seats may name a different model of the project's provider; a different provider only from the project's own `providers_allowed` list (for F-20's second reviewer). A `client` project never falls back to Z.ai or to any provider outside its list on error, quota or a missing credential: the session fails closed with the reason named. Tests cover the allowed override, the refused override and the no-fallback path.

The importer and `factory eval` take the same provider resolution as `factory run` (one resolver, no second code path). A test runs the importer's session construction for a `client` project and asserts the resolved provider, env and egress match AC-1 to AC-3.

One real session per newly supported kind the owner has provisioned (at minimum `bedrock`, EU region, Sonnet 5.5) runs against the rehearsal fixture (F-24); its record shows the provider, region and token usage, and egress logs show no other model host. The owner runs it (paid) and records the evidence.

check.expect: owner tick evidence: the real session's record (provider, region, token usage) and its egress log

acceptance.text: Each project has one store at `<factory_root>/memory/<project>/entries.jsonl`, validated against `schema/memory.schema.json` on load (F-02); an invalid store refuses the run with the line named. An entry has `id`, `kind` (`repo_fact` | `finding_pattern` | `reviewer_calibration` | `attempt_note`), `text`, `sources` (run ids, with turn where one applies), `model` (the seat model it was learned under, from the F-59 provider record), `created`, `last_confirmed`, and optional `supersedes`. The file is append-only: a change is a new entry that supersedes the old one, and retiring an entry appends a retirement. A test rewrites a past line and asserts the load refuses.

Only the owner's `factory memory add | retire | confirm | redact` commands write the store, each under the store lock and only if the store's content hash still matches the one the command read, so two writes never clobber each other (the optimistic-write pattern Anthropic's memory stores use). No seat, tool, route or session writes it, it is outside every sandbox write allowlist, and a scripted session of each seat leaves the file byte-identical (the F-37 AC-4 pattern). F-19 and AC-6 produce drafts under `drafts/`, which are never served.

Each seat gets its own slice, built into its prompt by the orchestrator, never read from a path the session can reach. Implementer: `repo_fact`, `finding_pattern`, `attempt_note`. Reviewer and verifier: `repo_fact`, `finding_pattern`, `reviewer_calibration`, and never an `attempt_note` or any text an implementer session wrote. A session for one project never gets another project's entries. Tests assert each seat's built prompt and the cross-project refusal.

An entry is served only while it is fresh: its `model` matches the seat's resolved model and `last_confirmed` is within `memory.max_age_days` (`project.yaml`, default 30). A stale entry is withheld, never served with a warning, and `factory status` lists it as needing `factory memory confirm`. Tests cover a model change, an aged entry and a confirmed one.

The served slice has a size cap per seat (`memory.max_chars`, schema field, default 8000). A store whose fresh slice exceeds it refuses the run with the overflow named, so curation happens before the run, never by silent truncation. A test covers the refusal.

`factory memory seed <project>` drafts a repo map (layout, entry points, where tests live) from a read-only session with no repo write access and no GitHub token, and writes it to `drafts/` for the owner to read and add. A test asserts the seat's sandbox settings and that nothing is served until `add`.

`factory memory calibrate <run-id> --finding <n> --agree | --disagree --note <text>` records a `reviewer_calibration` entry that cites the run and the finding, so the reviewer's reference examples are the owner's own past judgements. The reviewer slice carries the most recent entries up to the AC-5 cap. A test asserts the entry and its place in the reviewer prompt.

Every session record lists the entry ids it was served and the store's content hash, and the F-30 trace carries both, so F-19 can attribute failures to entries the way it attributes them to `prompt_versions`. A test covers the record.

Memory text passes the F-43 egress redaction seam before it reaches a provider, like any other prompt content. A test seeds an entry with a credential-shaped string and asserts it never reaches the session's built input.

`factory memory redact <id>` replaces an entry's `text` with `[redacted]` and records when and why, keeping its id, sources and place in the file. It is the one permitted in-place change: a client's erasure request, or a secret that slipped in, must be removable, and the record that something was there must stay. A test asserts the redacted text is gone from the file and from every built prompt, and that the AC-1 append-only check still passes.

The sandbox launcher resolves only from trusted paths. `run_sandboxed` and the pin check (`ensure_srt`/`_verified_srt`) exec srt as `[node, <realpath of srt's cli.js>, ...]`; `node` is resolved once from the orchestrator's own PATH to an absolute path that lies outside every run dir and the factory root, and any other node is refused with the reason named. The pin check runs exactly the argv the launch uses. srt runs with a launcher environment, never the confined child's: the child's PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV reach only the confined command, as a shell assignment prefix the way TMPDIR already does. On Linux, `bwrapPath`/`socatPath` in the srt settings are absolute paths resolved the same way. Tests: a gate command that writes `<run>/.venv/bin/node` (and `bwrap`, `socat`) does not change what the next `run_sandboxed` launches; a node under a run dir is refused; the pin-check argv equals the launch argv.

Pushed content is scanned for the secrets the orchestrator holds. Before `push_branch`, every added line of `git diff --text <base>..<head>` and every commit message in `<base>..<head>` is scanned for each egress secret, literally and as its base64, hex and URL-encoded forms. A hit refuses the publish exactly like `check_pr_text`: nothing is pushed, the task escalates, and the reason names the file or commit but never echoes the secret. Tests: the token in a new file, in a modified file, in a commit message, and base64-encoded is refused each time; a clean diff pushes; the refusal text contains no secret.

Every factory-root path component built from a project name is a validated slug. `tasks.schema.json`'s `project` gets the profile's `^[a-z0-9-]+$` pattern; a queue whose `project` differs from the loaded profile's `name` refuses to load, with both names shown. Every path builder under the factory root goes through one helper that raises on a non-slug component instead of silently sanitising — runs, sandbox settings and their siblings, trace, progress, reports, import, eval, and the status/dashboard readers. Tests: `../x`, an absolute path, `a/b`, the empty string and a Unicode look-alike are refused at queue load and at each builder; the importer's repair path and `factory status` with such a queue create and read nothing outside `<root>/<area>/<slug>`.

tasks.title: Owner-held approval of project config and contracts

acceptance.text: Task approvals live in an owner ledger. `factory approve` (single and reconcile) appends to `<factory_root>/approvals/<project>.jsonl`; each entry holds the task id, a SHA-256 over the whole contract (every field except `status`, `acceptance_hash`, `approved_by`, `approved_at`, `attempts`, `attempt_resets`, `links`, and the tick-written completion fields of `owner_steps` (`done_at`, `done_by`, `evidence`)), `approved_by` and `approved_at`. `pick()` and run start return only tasks whose current contract hash matches a ledger entry; a `ready` task without a match is demoted to `draft`, with the reason named. An existing queue is adopted by one interactive owner command that shows each ready task and records it; it has no `--yes` for risk-flagged tasks, matching approve's rule. Tests: a hand-minted `ready` task with a correct `acceptance_hash` is never picked; an edit after approval to `risk`, `gates`, `budget`, `out_of_scope` or `acceptance` demotes the task; an approved task is picked; a ledger line rewritten in place refuses the load; ticking an owner step after approval does not demote.

The profile's security-relevant content is owner-approved. Keys covered: `commands.*`, `sentinels`, `network_allowlist`, `docs_allowlist`, `sandbox.*`, `repo.remote`, `repo.default_branch`, `repo.branch_protection`, `paths.protected`, `paths.risk`, `live_checks`, `toolkit`, and, once F-59 lands, its `provider` and `data_owner` blocks. These keys are hashed and must match an owner approval in the same ledger (`factory approve --profile`) before any session or gate runs; a changed profile refuses with the changed keys named. The approval prompt prints those keys, with network entries one per line. Tests cover the refusal for each key group, the approve path, and that unrelated keys don't need re-approval.

Egress entries for token-bearing sessions are exact hosts. `network_allowlist`/`docs_allowlist` entries must be bare hostnames: no wildcard, IP literal, port, scheme or path — anything else refuses the profile at load. The srt settings of every session seat (implementer, reviewer, verifier, importer) contain only the model host plus entries the owner approved under AC-2. Tests read the generated settings and cover each refused form.

Factory-control files are protected structurally. A schema-level default protected set holds `.factory/**` beside the runner-config globs; it is unioned in both seams that union runner config today — `apply_profile_defaults` and `check_diff_policy` — and a profile can widen protection but never remove it. Test: under a minimal profile with no `.factory` glob, an implementer edit to `.factory/project.yaml` yields `protected_path_touched`.

Every seat runs at a fixed turn cap the parent grants, never one derived from a session record (amended at spec review 2026-11-09, option D). The implementer gets `budget.max_turns`; every reviewer seat (round review, final review, each re-run) gets `REVIEWER_TURN_CAP` = 20; the verifier gets `VERIFIER_TURN_CAP` = 10. Review seats are never refused or shrunk on turns. Wall clock, measured by the parent, is the total bound: the implementer's window is `wall_clock_min` minus `REVIEW_WALL_RESERVE_MIN` = 15 (a floor, not a ceiling: review also gets every minute the implementer left), and a budget that cannot hold the reserve plus a 1-minute implementer window refuses at attempt start, naming the numbers. `record.num_turns` is telemetry only. Values owner-confirmed 2026-11-10. Test: a planted `num_turns` of 0 or 10**9 changes no seat's cap, the implementer's timeout is the budget minus the reserve, and a too-small wall budget refuses before any seat starts.

Free quota requeues are bounded. A quota-classified attempt is requeued without counting toward `max_attempts` at most 3 times per task per calendar day (UTC) and at most 9 times since the current attempt-budget floor (the lifetime cap was added in review; values owner-confirmed 2026-11-10), counted from the parent-written `started` stamps of the task's own attempt records (a missing, unparseable or offset-less stamp counts); beyond either allowance it counts as an attempt, and a record's `reason` alone never grants more. Test: repeated planted 429 records reach `attempts_exhausted` within `max_attempts` plus 3 runs.

Budgets are visible and bounded at approval. `render_contract` shows `max_turns`, `wall_clock_min` and `max_attempts`; the schema gains maxima — `max_turns` ≤ 200 and `wall_clock_min` ≤ 150 (the highest values in today's queue, so no existing entry fails to load; owner-confirmed 2026-11-10). Test: the rendered contract contains the three numbers, over-maximum values fail schema validation, and the factory's own `.factory/tasks.json` still validates.

Contracts declare their file scope. The task schema gains `scope.paths`: a non-empty list of repo-relative globs, inside `contract_hash`, so the F-63 approval ledger covers it and any widening needs re-approval. Scope globs use their own matcher: `*` and `?` never cross `/`, `**` matches across directories, matching is case-sensitive on the exact git path. Protected and risk paths keep today's matcher unchanged (its `*` crosses `/`, so it stays the broader, fail-safe one). A pattern that is absolute, contains `..`, is empty, or matches every path (`**`, `**/*`, `*/**` and equivalents) refuses to load, naming the task and the pattern. `render_contract` shows the paths. `scope` stays optional in the schema so existing entries load, but every task of a kind the picker runs (`ELIGIBLE_KINDS`: `build` and `docs` today) needs it, checked twice: approval refuses such a task without it, and so does the run itself, so a task approved before F-65 never starts a session without a scope; it escalates `scope_missing` (needs_human), naming the task. `owner_only` tasks run no session and are exempt. The importer proposes `scope.paths` for every task it drafts. Test: each refused shape refuses with the pattern named; the hash changes when a path changes; approval and the run each refuse a scope-less `build` task and a scope-less `docs` task, the run before any session starts; a scope-less `owner_only` task still approves; the factory's own `.factory/tasks.json` still validates.

L0 fails changes outside the declared scope. Every changed path, whether added, modified, deleted, mode-only, a submodule pointer, or either side of a rename or copy, must match `scope.paths`, a profile `paths.generated` glob (AC-4), or one of the task's own contract test files; anything else is an L0 FAIL finding that names the path and the scope. Scope never overrides protection: a protected path inside the scope still fails exactly as today. Paths are judged on the exact git path bytes: a case variant, a Unicode-normalisation look-alike, or a symlink whose own path is out of scope fails even when its target or folded form is in scope. F-65 governs which files change, not what changes inside them: unrelated edits inside an in-scope file stay the L2 reviewer's to catch against `out_of_scope`, so an L0 pass is never read as "scope verified". Test: one planted diff per change class, plus each bypass shape, and an all-in-scope diff that passes.

The implementer works inside its scope and asks instead of drifting. The implementer prompt lists `scope.paths`. A session that needs a file outside it ends with a structured scope request (each path with a one-line reason) instead of editing it, and the parent escalates `scope_change_needed` (needs_human) at once, showing the requested paths and reasons, so no round is spent on a revert. An out-of-scope change made without a request is an L0 finding the fix round sees as "revert it, or request the wider scope"; the same unrequested path in two rounds of one attempt escalates `scope_change_needed` too. `scope_change_needed` and `scope_missing` join the escalation enum. The owner widens the scope (or declines) and re-approves, and the re-approval returns the task to `ready` through the existing approval path; nothing inside a run can widen it, and a request never changes the stored scope by itself. Test: a scripted implementer that files a request escalates in round 1 with its paths and reasons shown and the stored scope unchanged; one that keeps touching an out-of-scope file unrequested escalates within 2 rounds with the path named; one that reverts in round 2 opens a PR.

Generated files are allowed explicitly, never implicitly. A project profile may declare `paths.generated` globs (lockfiles, snapshots, codegen output) that are in scope for every task of that project; they are owner-approved profile content under F-63 (security group) and obey AC-1's refused shapes. No other implicit allowance exists. Test: a lockfile change passes only when declared; a catch-all `paths.generated` refuses to load; widening `paths.generated` without re-approval refuses the run.

Rule changes are declared as contract epochs, and CI enforces the declaration. The epoch register is `factory/data/schema/epochs.json`, protected and schema-validated. It lists each epoch: number, date, the WO, the surfaces it tightens (`queue`, `profile`, or both), what changed in one line, and its migration. A migration is either a named automatic rewrite (AC-4) or an owner action, with the exact command. The current epoch is the register's highest number. It is stamped as the queue's top-level `version` on every factory write. Epoch 1 is today's baseline. Epochs 2–4 are registered retroactively for F-64, F-65 and F-59. A test fingerprints both schema files and the profile/queue semantic-check functions (`_check_semantics`, the provider and allowlist checks) against the register's latest entry. Any change to them without a new register entry fails CI with the instruction to add one. An entry that tightens nothing (a refactor, a loosening) records that and does not raise the epoch. Test: editing either schema file, or a fingerprinted function, without a register entry fails. The same edit with an entry passes. The factory's own queue carries the current epoch.

`factory doctor` checks every onboarded project, read-only, before anything breaks mid-run. The F-63 approval ledger records the repo path with each profile approval. Doctor checks every repo in the ledger, plus any `--repo` given. For each repo it loads the profile and queue through the real loaders, collecting ALL violations instead of stopping at the first (an all-errors mode of `validate_queue`/`load_profile`). It reports: schema and semantic violations, each with its epoch and migration; tasks of a runnable kind that approval would refuse (`scope_missing`, over-cap budgets); a profile whose approved group hashes no longer match its file; the queue's recorded epoch against the current one. It starts no session, writes nothing, and exits non-zero on any finding. `factory run`, `loop` and `import` run the same checks for their own repo first, and refuse with doctor's full report instead of one bare schema error. Test: a planted pre-F-64 queue, a scope-less queue and a profile with a banned allowlist host are each reported with the epoch and the exact fix. A clean repo exits 0. Nothing under the factory root or the repo changes.

A stale project names its way forward. Every refusal caused by a rule newer than the file says which epoch the file predates, what changed, and the command that fixes it (the register's migration). It never ends as only `schema violation at tasks/31/...`. Test: the F-13 pilot's two refusals (the over-cap queue, the `docs.z.ai` profile) each print the epoch, the WO and the fix command.

A draft-only stale queue is re-proposed, never patched. If the existing queue fails validation but still parses as JSON, and every task in it is `draft`, `factory import` proposes a full replacement under the current rules. The owner reviews it exactly as a first import: the whole diff against the old file, every line. Any task past `draft` (approved, in flight, done or escalated), or a file that does not parse, refuses the re-proposal, naming those tasks and the epoch they predate. Those need the owner's per-task action. Owner-confirmed automatic rewrites named in the register are the only edits a migration may make without a session, and only ones that cannot change a task's meaning (for example, re-stamping `version` on a queue that already validates under the current rules). None of them may touch an approved task's hashed contract fields. Test: a draft-only queue with over-cap budgets re-imports through a scripted importer into a valid current-epoch queue, and the review shows the full diff. The same queue with one approved task refuses, naming it. An approved task's `contract_hash` is never changed by any migration.

tasks.title: Importer v0 gates, session record and shipped-work flag

acceptance.text: Imported gates are human in v0. Every task the importer writes, new or merged, has `merge: human` and `deploy: human`, and every task of a kind the picker runs (`ELIGIBLE_KINDS`) has `spec_approval: true`, whatever the proposal says. A proposed relaxation is never silently dropped: the review output lists each one per task (field, proposed value, stored value) before the diff. The importer prompt states all three rules. `factory approve` refuses a task whose `merge` or `deploy` is not `human`, naming it, so a hand-edited or legacy queue cannot carry an auto gate into a run either; `owner_only` tasks keep whatever `spec_approval` they have. Test: a scripted proposal with `deploy: auto` and `spec_approval: false` on a build task lands all-human with the overrides listed; approve refuses a planted `deploy: auto`; the factory's own queue and a queue with `spec_approval: false` on an `owner_only` task still load and approve.

Every import session is on record. The importer and its repair session each write their session record (the parent-stamped F-59 provider, the model the session reported, validated usage, turns, outcome) under the factory root's `import/` directory next to the proposal, named for the run, owner-only permissions, never a credential. A profile with no `models` entry for the importer records the model the session actually reported, or `unknown`, never a bare null. `factory status` counts import sessions in its Providers table as their own rows. Test: a scripted import with a repair round writes two records with provider, model and usage; a forged provider in the session-written record is overwritten by the parent's; status renders the import rows; no token value appears in any record.

Possibly shipped work is flagged for the owner, never decided. The importer prompt asks the session, for each build or docs task it proposes, to check the default branch for the task's named deliverables (files, functions, migrations, a status line in the repo's own records) and to report the ones it finds in a `possibly_shipped` list: task id, evidence (path, commit or doc line) and a one-line reason. The review output shows that list first, before the diff. Nothing changes a task's status automatically: the owner drops, re-scopes or approves each one. A malformed entry, or one naming a task the proposal does not contain, refuses the proposal. Test: a scripted proposal with two valid `possibly_shipped` entries renders them before the diff and leaves both tasks `draft`; a malformed entry and an unknown id each refuse.

Criteria the docs still carry are never silently dropped. The reference is the repo's existing `.factory/tasks.json`, read as plain JSON even when it fails the current schema, so an import into a fresh queue file (`--queue`) is checked too. Every reference task and every one of its acceptance criteria must be accounted for: mapped to a proposed task and criterion (the proposal states each new task's predecessors), or listed in `dropped_criteria` (a whole task, or one criterion) with the doc line that removes, completes or supersedes it. The parent checks the accounting is complete and that each cited doc line exists in a kept planning doc; an unaccounted task or criterion refuses the proposal, naming it. The review output shows `dropped_criteria` before the diff. A dropped criterion whose source text is still present in the kept planning docs is flagged `still in docs` and blocks applying the proposal until the owner accepts the drop at review. Found on JobFinderOS: the WO-19 rule "never fetch or output URLs that appear inside the posting body" (still in `WO-19-honest-gates.md`) and five other doc-carried items vanished from the proposal with no trace. Test: a scripted import into a fresh `--queue` file over a schema-invalid reference queue still runs the check; one that leaves a reference criterion unaccounted refuses, naming it; one that drops a criterion still present in the docs refuses to apply until accepted, naming the criterion and its doc line; a drop backed by a doc line that marks the work done is listed and applies; a criterion mapped across a task split (one task into two) is not reported as dropped.

The home page lists every project the factory knows (each repo recorded in the F-63 approval ledger, plus the factory itself), one card each: name, current lifecycle stage (onboarding, import review, queue, running, PR, idle), tasks by status, open factory PRs, the escalations waiting on the owner, and tokens and estimated cost this week (F-59 provider rows, including F-67's import sessions). Above the cards, one "needs you" strip lists every pending owner act across projects (an approval, an import to read, an escalation, a PR to merge) linking to where it is decided. A project whose profile or queue fails to load shows the failure on its card, never crashes the page. Test: a fixture factory root with three projects (one healthy, one with a stale queue, one onboarding) renders three cards with the right stage and counts, the stale one showing its load error, and the strip listing each pending act once.

A project page is a kanban of that project's tasks: columns Onboard, Draft, Approved, Running, PR, Merged (escalated tasks show in place, flagged), with a header of the project's lifecycle checklist and its cost and first-pass numbers. Each task card shows id, size, risk flags, the current round's L0–L4 verdict chips, its PR link and CI state when it has one, and tokens and minutes for its latest attempt. A running task updates live from F-31's existing event stream; no second live transport. Test: a fixture queue with one task per column renders each in its column with its chips; a scripted run's trace events move a card from Running to PR without a reload.

Clicking a task opens a drawer with its whole history: the contract as `render_contract` shows it, each attempt and round with its verdicts and findings, the trace for that run, the PR, and cost. Every step opens with a one-line plain summary, the raw detail below it. Every text shown that came from a session (findings, notes, summaries, PR bodies) goes through `escape_approval_text`. Test: a fixture task with two attempts and a failed L2 round renders both with summaries first; a finding carrying ESC/CSI/bidi bytes renders escaped.

Still read-only and still local: every new route is GET, Host-checked (F-31 AC-2), builds no filesystem path from URL input, and serves only from the factory root and the recorded repos. A test sweeps every route against a fixture root and asserts no file under it or under any recorded repo changed (mtime and hash), and that a `..`, absolute or symlinked project path is refused.

Start and confirm are the only writes, and only the owner's click makes either happen. The dashboard gains exactly two POST routes: `POST /onboard/start` (starts an onboarding session for a named new project) and `POST /onboard/confirm` (carries out one proposed write). Both enforce F-34 AC-2's per-launch token, exact `Host` and matching `Origin`; a confirm carries a one-time nonce bound to the proposal's kind and the hash of its exact content, and a reused nonce or changed content gets 409 and writes nothing. The confirm card is built by the server from the onboarding state file, never from agent text (F-35 AC-2). No agent tool, route or token reaches `/onboard/confirm`. Test: one test per refusal (token, Host, Origin, reused nonce, changed content); a scripted session that tries every tool leaves everything outside its own state file byte-identical; one end-to-end start and confirm from a page served as `localhost`.

The interview asks every gate question before anything is written, and records each answer in `<factory_root>/onboarding/<project>/state.json` (0600 in 0700): whose project it is (`data_owner`); the model provider and region, refusing a choice F-59 would refuse at load (a client with Z.ai); for a client, whether a DPA or written consent is on file; whether a repo exists (GitHub remote, local folder only, or nothing), and if nothing, the stack and the GitHub account (F-70); setup, lint, typecheck and test commands; where the plan lives and whether the planning docs are current with what has shipped; protected and risk paths; the deploy target (deploy gate always human in v0); docs and network allowlists; default budgets within the F-64 caps; an optional monthly cost cap. Answers the repo already holds (commands from its CI files, dependencies, existing protected paths, default branch) are detected and shown for the owner to confirm, never assumed. Test: a scripted interview over a fixture repo detects its CI commands and asks only the rest; a client + Z.ai answer is refused with the F-59 reason; nothing is written before the last answer.

Each answer is carried out as a proposed write the owner confirms: the adapter (`.factory/project.yaml`), the data-processing record (`.factory/data-processing.md`), a branch and PR in the project repo carrying both, and the keychain item check (presence only, never the value). Every proposed adapter passes `load_profile` and `factory doctor` (F-66) before its card is shown; a failing one is fixed in the session, never shown. Nothing is pushed to the default branch. Test: a scripted onboarding produces exactly these proposals; a confirmed adapter loads clean; a declined one writes nothing; an adapter that `factory doctor` flags is never offered.

Onboarding runs every check the F-13 pilot hit and shows each result on the project's checklist (F-68): the provider credential is present; `gh` can push to the repo; the default branch has the protection and required checks the factory admits (F-26); the local checkout is clean; open PRs that touch the same files as onboarding's own PR are listed; the readiness run passes every profile command unattended in the real sandbox on a clean clone; `factory doctor` is clean. A failing check names the exact fix and blocks the next step; nothing is silently skipped. Test: one fixture per failing check shows its named fix and blocks; an all-passing fixture reaches the next step.

Onboarding ends at ready for the first run: it runs the import (F-67, a session the owner confirms starting), shows the import review (possibly shipped, dropped criteria, gate overrides, the diff) for the owner to accept, then proposes the best first task with its acceptance refs and `scope.paths` already checked for approvability (exact test refs, tight scope, no catch-all) and the reasons it was chosen. The owner's three acts (`factory approve --profile`, accepting the import, approving the first task) are shown as the exact command or confirm card, never taken. Test: a scripted onboarding over a fixture repo with a planning doc reaches "ready for first run" with the three owner acts pending and nothing approved; the proposed first task passes `_check_approvable`.

Stack templates ship in the factory package, vetted and versioned. The first is the owner's default stack: a FastAPI backend with PostgreSQL/Supabase access, pytest with one passing test, ruff, a GitHub Actions CI workflow running lint and tests, a README and a `docs/` folder for the plan. Each template declares the adapter commands it implies. Test: rendering the template into a temp dir and running its declared setup, lint and test commands passes, offline except for package installs.

Creating the repo is a confirmed write (F-69 AC-1): onboarding proposes the repo name, the owner's chosen GitHub account, private visibility and the default branch, and only the confirm creates the GitHub repo, makes the first commit of the rendered skeleton, pushes it, and sets branch protection with the template's CI as a required check. A local folder that already exists is used as the working copy only when it is empty or holds no git repo; otherwise onboarding stops and names the clash. Test: with the GitHub CLI stubbed, a confirm issues exactly those calls in order; a decline issues none; a non-empty folder with a repo stops with the clash named.

A scaffolded project then goes through F-69's checks unchanged: the generated adapter loads and passes `factory doctor`, the readiness run passes on a clean clone, and its CI is green on the first commit. Test: a scaffold into a temp repo with a stubbed remote passes `load_profile`, `factory doctor` and the readiness run.

tasks.title: Pre-spend contract checks and dependency policy

acceptance.text: Risk flags cover the scope. At approval, and on every task the importer writes, the factory computes the risk flags the contract's `scope.paths` can reach. It takes every tracked file on the default branch that matches a scope glob, plus each literal scope path, and runs them through the profile's `paths.risk` matcher (the same matcher L0 uses). The importer adds any missing flag to the task's `risk` and lists each addition at review. Approval refuses a contract whose `risk` does not cover the computed flags, naming each flag and the scope path that reaches it. Test: a contract scoping a profile risk path without its flag is refused at approval with the flag and path named. The importer adds the flag and lists it. A contract that declares the flag approves. A scope glob that reaches a risk file only through `**` is caught too.

Check refs are runnable before approval. Approval refuses a `test` check whose `ref` is not `<repo-relative path>::<test name>` (one or more `::` segments), and a `command` check whose command is empty. It warns, without refusing, on a ref whose file sits under the profile's `paths.protected` while the scope cannot touch that file. The warning names the criterion: it can go green only through a protected change (the wo19 calibration-pin case). The owner must confirm the warning at the y/N prompt. `--yes` is refused for a task carrying the warning. The importer prompt requires exact refs and states the convention for new test files (`tests/test_<task>.py::test_ac_N`). Test: a prose ref refuses with the criterion named. An exact ref approves. A ref into a protected file outside scope shows the warning, and `--yes` is refused for it. The factory's own queue still approves.

Budgets have a floor the owner sets once. The profile gains an optional `budget_floor` (`max_turns`, default 60; `wall_clock_min`, default 30), owner-approved profile content under F-63. It stays inside F-64's caps, and a floor above a cap refuses to load. Approval refuses a runnable task below the floor, naming the field, and the importer clamps a proposal up to the floor and lists the change. Test: a 30-turn task refuses at approval under the default floor. The importer clamps a 30-turn proposal to 60 and lists it. A floor of 300 refuses to load.

Declared dependencies pass without a human. The task schema gains an optional `dependencies` list, inside `contract_hash`: each entry has `ecosystem` (`pypi` or `npm`) and `name`. When a diff changes a `dependency_manifests` file, L0 parses what was added: direct requirements from `requirements*.txt`, `pyproject.toml` dependency tables and `package.json` dependency maps, and every new pin in `requirements*.lock` and `package-lock.json`. Every added direct package must be declared in the contract. A changed version of an already-pinned package counts as added. Every added package, direct or transitive, must pass the registry checks VALIDATOR-SPEC L0 deferred: it exists in its registry, its first release is at least 30 days old, and its name is not within edit distance 1 of a package on the top-package list shipped in the factory package (and is not that package). The checks run parent-side, outside the sandbox, against the public registry's JSON API, and their results are recorded in the L0 report. A declared direct package that passes every check no longer escalates `new_dependency`. An undeclared package, a failed check, an unreadable registry, or a manifest L0 cannot parse escalates as today (fail closed). Approval shows the declared dependencies, and `--yes` is refused for a contract that declares any. Test: with the registry stubbed, a declared, aged package with an unrelated name passes L0 with no escalation. Each of these escalates: undeclared, too new, a near-miss name, registry down, an unparseable lockfile. A transitive pin that fails a check escalates even though its parent is declared.

tasks.title: Escalations keep the work, retry first, and never stop the batch

acceptance.text: Guarded changes retry before they escalate. A `protected_path_touched` or `sentinel_failed` result becomes an L0 FAIL finding for the next fix round of the same attempt. The finding names the path or the sentinel output and the instruction ("revert this; it is outside what this contract may change"). Only the same class on the same path or sentinel in 2 consecutive rounds escalates, with its reason, and the escalation note says the contract or the project rule is the likely problem. F-65's handling of out-of-scope changes is unchanged: an explicit scope request still escalates at once, because it means the contract is too narrow. `credential_added` keeps its immediate escalation and is never retried. Test: a scripted implementer that touches a protected file in round 1 and reverts in round 2 reaches a PR. One that touches it in both rounds escalates `protected_path_touched` within 2 rounds. A failing sentinel follows the same pattern. A credential still escalates in round 1.

An arbiter settles a non-converging review before the owner. Where `review_not_converging` fires today, the parent first starts an arbiter session. It runs in a seat of its own under a fixed parent-side turn cap (F-64), and gets the contract, the diff and only the repeated findings, never the implementer's or reviewer's argument. For each finding it rules: `valid` (one more fix round must resolve it), `invalid` (dropped from this attempt's review), or `contract` (the contract itself is wrong). It rules through a structured tool, in the same way as the reviewer's verdict. A `contract` ruling, a second non-convergence after an arbiter ruling, or an arbiter session that fails escalates `review_not_converging` with the rulings attached. Test: scripted rulings of all-`invalid` lead to a PR. A `valid` ruling leads to one more round. A `contract` ruling escalates with the ruling shown. A failed arbiter session escalates.

An escalation after a session keeps the work as a draft PR. When a run escalates after a session produced commits, the parent pushes the run branch and opens a draft PR through the existing push fence and PR-body gates. The body names the escalation, links the stored L0–L2 reports, and carries the factory's escalation label. `links.pr` records it. The task is `needs_human` as today, and the clone is cleaned only after the push succeeds. `credential_added` never pushes; its branch is discarded as today. A failed push or PR create leaves the reports on disk and records `pr_create_failed` with the reason. An escalation draft PR never counts as a ready factory PR: the sweep does not re-validate it, and `factory run` never reports it `ready`. Test: a scripted `new_dependency` escalation opens one draft PR with the reason and links, and the task links it. A `credential_added` escalation pushes nothing. A stubbed push failure records `pr_create_failed` and keeps the reports.

The owner answers an escalation in one command. `factory recover <task-id> --accept --evidence "<what you checked>"` is interactive y/N with no `--yes`, and it is accepted for `new_dependency` and `risk_path_touched` escalations that hold an escalation draft PR. It records the acceptance (task, escalation, PR head SHA, evidence, who, when) in the approval ledger. It then re-runs L0 on that exact head with that escalation class waived for that SHA only, and continues the round through L1 and review. A pass marks the PR ready for review and the task `in_review`. Any new commit on the branch voids the waiver. `factory recover <task-id> --reject` closes the draft PR and returns the task to `draft` (a new `needs_human → draft` edge in the transition table), so the contract can be changed and re-approved. The other escalation reasons keep their current exits. Test: an accepted `new_dependency` on an unchanged head reaches `in_review` with the ledger entry written. The same accept after a new commit refuses. An accept for a `protected_path_touched` escalation refuses with the supported reasons named. A reject closes the PR and drafts the task.

The loop parks an escalation and carries on. `factory loop` no longer stops on `needs_human`. It parks the task and picks the next eligible one, and it still stops on an empty queue, quota, the peak window, or an orchestrator error. An escalation draft PR does not hold the repo's writer slot. At the end, the loop prints one line per task parked during the run: id, reason, and the draft PR. Test: a scripted queue of three tasks where the first escalates runs the second and third, then prints the parked one. An orchestrator error still stops the loop.

tasks.title: Ready clones: the factory's identity and setup before the session

acceptance.text: The clone is ready before the session. In each attempt, after the run branch is checked out and before the implementer's first session, the parent: - sets the factory's commit identity (the same name and email the orchestrator commits with) as repo-local git config in the clone; - runs the profile's `commands.setup` there, with the same runner, sandbox and timeout L0 uses for setup. The implementer prompt says setup has run, names the command, and says commits are made as the configured identity, never another. A setup that exits non-zero, or that leaves tracked files modified or untracked files git does not ignore, starts no session. The attempt is recorded failed with reason `setup_failed`, the output tail and the dirty paths. That failure spends no attempt budget (no session ran) and stops `factory loop` like an orchestrator error, because a broken setup fails every task. Test: a scripted setup that creates a gitignored venv lets a scripted implementer commit as the factory identity and see the venv. A failing setup starts no session, records `setup_failed`, and leaves the attempt budget unchanged. A setup that writes an un-ignored file refuses, naming it.

Nothing is published under another identity. Before any push (the validated publish and the F-72 escalation push), the parent checks the author and committer of every commit in base..head. If any is not the factory identity, the branch is rebuilt as one commit on the base under the factory identity. This uses F-72's squash with its tree assertion: the tree pushed is exactly the validated tree. The attempt record notes the foreign identities found (escaped). The run is not failed: the content was validated, and only the attribution is corrected. Test: a scripted implementer that commits with `-c user.name=<other> -c user.email=<other>` reaches a PR whose pushed history carries only the factory identity, with the validated tree unchanged, and the note names the foreign identity. A run whose commits are all factory-authored keeps its round commits, so this never squashes unnecessarily.

Failed sessions keep their usage. When the SDK raises after it has delivered a `ResultMessage` (`ResultError` on `error_max_turns`, `error_during_execution`, an API error result), the session record is built from that message: `status: failed`, the reason, `num_turns`, model, usage and cost exactly as for a completed session, through the same validation (F-64 telemetry, F-59 provider stamp). A failure with no result delivered (wall clock, a transport error before any result) keeps today's bare record, and its usage renders `unknown`, never 0, in the trace, the attempt record and `factory status`. Test: a scripted stream that yields an error `ResultMessage` and then raises `ResultError` produces a record with the message's turns, model and usage; the trace's `session_end` carries them; `factory status` sums them into the week's quota line. A stream that raises with no prior result renders `unknown`, and the week's total is marked partial rather than silently lower.

A retry resumes from what the last attempt left. When an attempt starts on a branch that already carries commits from an earlier attempt of the same run, its prompt gains a handoff section the parent builds: - the previous attempt's outcome and reason; - the branch's commits since the base (subject lines and a diffstat, capped); - the current red/green of every contract check, which the parent runs on the branch head with L1's runner before the session starts. Commit subjects and test output are session-originated: they go in under the prompt's untrusted-data framing, escaped and capped. The section says the branch already holds the earlier work and the session continues it. Test: a scripted attempt 1 that commits a green AC-1 and dies at max turns gives attempt 2 a prompt showing that commit, AC-1 green, the other criteria red, and the max-turns reason. A commit subject carrying instructions or ESC/bidi bytes renders escaped under the untrusted heading. 500 commits stay within the cap.

tasks.title: CI is part of done: a red PR gets a fix round

acceptance.text: The run waits for its PR's CI. After a validated publish opens or updates a PR, the parent polls the checks on the exact pushed SHA until every check settles, or until `ci_wait_min` (config, default 30) passes. All green: the run ends `pr_opened` as today. No checks reported on the SHA after the window: `pr_opened` with the note "no CI reported", the ready rule's current behaviour. Window spent with checks still pending: `pr_opened` with the note "CI pending", and AC-3 decides readiness later. The wait counts against the run's wall clock, not its session turns. Test: scripted check states (green, red, pending until timeout, none) on the exact SHA produce each outcome. A check reported for a different SHA is ignored.

Red CI becomes a fix round on the same branch. When any check fails, the parent first re-runs the failed jobs once, because CI flakes are real (the pilot hit one). Only a second red counts. Then the next implementer round starts on the PR branch's head, in the same clone, with findings for each failing check: its name and the failing log's tail (`gh run view --log-failed`). The tail is capped, scrubbed of run secrets and escaped, under the prompt's untrusted-data framing, because CI output is produced by code a session wrote. The round counts against `max_attempts` and runs L0, L1 and review as usual. Its push updates the same PR through the same push fence, as a fast-forward, never a force-push, and CI is awaited again. If attempts run out with CI still red, the task goes `needs_human` with a new escalation `ci_failed`: the PR stays open (converted to draft), and the note names the failing checks and the stored log tail. Test: a scripted CI that is red on head 1 and green on head 2 gives one fix round whose prompt carries the failing check and its log tail, then `pr_opened` on the same PR URL. A flake (red, then green on re-run) gives no fix round. Red on every head exhausts to `ci_failed` with the PR drafted. A log tail carrying instructions or ESC/bidi bytes renders escaped under the untrusted heading.

Nothing is reported ready on red or unknown CI. `factory run` and the sweep report a factory PR `ready` only when every check on its current head is green. This extends F-58's green-CI rule from `branch_protection: unavailable` repos to every repo. A PR whose CI went red after the run ended (the AC-1 pending case, or a later re-run) is listed as `not ready: CI red` with the failing check names, and it waits for the owner. Test: a PR with a red check on its head is never in the ready list, on a protected repo and an unprotected one alike, and the not-ready line names the check.

tasks.title: Stale-base re-validation: re-run once, a way back for an open PR, and a fix round for a PR that goes red later

acceptance.text: A failing re-validation runs once more before it parks. When L0 or L1 on the merged tree fails a command (setup, lint, typecheck, test or an extra command exits non-zero), the sweep re-runs L0 and L1 once on a fresh clean clone of the same merged SHA, with the same runner and timeout. Only a second failure escalates `stale_base`. The stored `<run-id>-revalidate.json` keeps both runs, and the note says it failed twice. A pass on the re-run is a pass: `links.revalidated` is stamped as today, and the progress entry names the first run's failing findings as "failed once, passed on re-run" so a flaky test stays visible. A merge conflict and L0 escalations (e.g. `new_dependency`, `protected_path_touched`) are deterministic, so they never re-run and park as today. The re-run must not be able to turn a real failure green: it gets a fresh clean clone of the merged SHA and never reuses the first run's tree, venv, caches or temp files. Test: a scripted gate runner that fails then passes gives no escalation, stamps `links.revalidated` and writes a progress note naming the flaked finding. Fails twice gives `stale_base` with both runs in the report. A merge conflict runs nothing and parks. An L0 escalation parks after one run. A deterministic failure that leaves state behind in the first clone (a file the second run would read) still fails twice.

A parked stale_base PR can be re-validated on the owner's word, keeping its work. `factory recover <task-id> --revalidate` takes a task parked on `stale_base` whose PR GitHub reports open, and runs the sweep's re-validation of the PR's current head against the current remote default head: the same code path including AC-1's re-run, not a copy. Pass: the task moves `needs_human → in_review`, `links.revalidated` is stamped, and the progress log gains an entry (outcome `recovered`, the default SHA, the report name, `done_by`). From there the PR is reported ready or not ready by the F-75 CI rule like any in_review PR. Fail: the task stays `needs_human`, the new report is stored, and the command exits non-zero naming the failing step. The edge is written only by a dedicated state-layer method, gated to a `stale_base` escalation holding an open PR link and a passing re-validation of that exact (PR head, default head) pair. The generic transition and the sweep still refuse it. Refused, with nothing written: any other escalation, a closed or merged PR (the existing edges own those), or a PR state gh cannot answer (fails closed). No model session runs and no attempt is spent. The command takes the run lease like every queue writer and asks no confirmation: a passing re-validation is the evidence, so it needs no y/N. Docs: TASK-CONTRACT's recovery table and the `stale_base` paragraph, and VALIDATOR-SPEC's merge-order paragraph, name the re-run and the new exit. Test: a parked task whose open PR re-validates clean goes to in_review with the stamp and a `recovered` log entry. A failing re-validation leaves it parked with a stored report and a non-zero exit. A `pr_closed`, `credential_added` or closed-PR `stale_base` task is refused untouched. An unknown PR state is refused. The generic `needs_human → in_review` transition still refuses a `stale_base` task.

A factory PR in review whose CI settles red gets F-75's fix round. When the sweep has proved an in-review factory PR current (up to date, re-validated or cached for the current default head) and its CI on that head has settled red (every check finished, at least one failed: F-75's settle rule, never a pending or unresolvable state), it runs F-75's flake guard once per head (re-run the failed Actions jobs, wait again). If the PR is still red, the task takes F-75's CI fix round on that PR: the `in_review → in_progress` fix-round edge, a clone of the PR branch's head, one finding per failing check (name plus the capped, scrubbed, escaped `--log-failed` tail under the untrusted-data heading), L0, L1 and review as usual, a fast-forward leased push through the push fence that updates the same PR, then F-75's CI wait. The round reuses F-75's code in `factory/ci.py` and the orchestrator; it does not copy it. It counts against `max_attempts`. With the budget already spent, no session runs: the task goes `needs_human` on `ci_failed` with the PR converted to draft, as F-75 exhausts today. It acts only when the PR's head is the SHA the factory last pushed or validated. A head moved by anyone else is reported (`not ready: head moved outside the factory`) and never built on. The peak window and the one-open-PR concurrency rule apply as for any run, and at most one sweep fix round starts per run. An F-72 escalation draft PR, a merged PR and a parked task are never touched. Docs: the TASK-CONTRACT and VALIDATOR-SPEC prose that says a red in-review PR waits for the owner is updated. F-75's own spec text stays as built history. Test: an in-review PR red on its head gets one flake re-run, then a fix round whose prompt carries the failing check and its tail, and its push updates the same PR URL. Red then green on the re-run gives no fix round and a `ready` line. Pending or unresolvable gives no action. A spent budget gives `ci_failed` with the PR drafted and no session. A head pushed by someone else gives no fix round and the not-ready line. An escalation draft PR and the peak window give no fix round.

tasks.title: A ci_failed PR gets more budget without losing its work

acceptance.text: A `ci_failed` budget reset keeps an open PR. `factory recover <task-id> --reset-attempts --evidence "…"` on a task parked `ci_failed` reads the PR's state from GitHub. Open: the task moves `needs_human → in_review` (not `ready`) with the same `attempt_resets` marker the reset writes today, so the attempt budget counts from zero; `links` (`pr`, `branch`, `pushed_head`, `revalidated`, `ci_rerun_heads`) are untouched; the drafted PR is marked ready again, and a failure of that gh call after the state write is reported loudly without failing the command. Closed: today's behaviour (`ready`, or `blocked` on an open dependency; a fresh run re-implements). Merged, or a state gh cannot answer: refused with the reason named, nothing written. An `attempts_exhausted` task is unchanged. The gate lives in the state layer, in the one writer of the marker: only a `needs_human` task whose last attempt escalated `ci_failed` and which holds a normal `links.pr` (no `links.escalation_pr`) can take the `in_review` target, and the generic transition still refuses it. Evidence, the interactive y/N and the `--yes` refusal stay as they are; the echo before the y/N says which outcome will happen (keep the PR and fix it in place, or re-implement from the default head); the keep-the-PR move takes the run lease; the progress log gains the `recovered` entry (escalation `ci_failed`, the target status, the PR URL).

The next sweep runs the fix round on that PR. A task parked `ci_failed` with a spent budget, an open red PR, `links.pushed_head` equal to the remote head and that head already in `links.ci_rerun_heads`, once recovered per AC-1, gets F-75's CI fix round from the next run's sweep on the same PR URL, its prompt carrying the failing check; the head is not re-run a second time; and when the fresh budget is spent too with CI still red, the task parks `ci_failed` again with the PR drafted. The edge composes with F-75/F-76's machinery; no fix-round logic is forked.

The parked line names the PR. `factory loop`'s `parked:` line prints the task's PR for a sweep park too (`ci_failed`, `stale_base`, `pr_closed`): the normal `links.pr`, or the escalation draft PR as today. It prints "no PR" only when the task holds neither link. The PR is carried on the run's result where it is built, so `factory run` and `factory loop` agree, and GitHub is not re-read for it.
